Our analysis reveals that the model strongly learns to identify hypernyms using Hearst patterns, which are well-known to be predictive of lexical relations. Hearst patterns are a set of linguistic patterns that were first introduced by Hearst (1992) and have been widely used to identify hypernyms in text. For example, the pattern "X such as Y" is a strong indicator of a hypernym-hyponym relationship between X and Y. We find that the existing model is able to capture these patterns in the distributional vectors, which enables it to identify hypernyms with high accuracy. However, the model does not explicitly exploit these patterns as a method of feature extraction. To address this limitation, we propose a novel model that combines the strengths of the existing model with the power of Hearst patterns. Our model uses an iterative procedure similar to Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to extract features from the distributional vectors. In each iteration, the model identifies the most informative features that are correlated with the Hearst patterns and uses them to update the vector representations of the words. This process allows the model to capture the nuances of the lexical relations and improve its performance on the task of predicting lexical entailment. We evaluate our model on multiple datasets and show that it matches or outperforms prior work.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) that involves identifying and categorizing named entities in unstructured text into predefined categories such as person, organization, and location. The importance of NER cannot be overstated, as it has numerous applications in information extraction, question answering, sentiment analysis, and machine translation, among others. With the advent of deep learning techniques, NER systems have achieved remarkable performance, often rivaling human-level accuracy. However, these systems typically require large amounts of manually labeled training data, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain. To mitigate the need for manually labeled data, researchers have turned to distant supervision, which involves using external dictionaries or knowledge bases to automatically generate labels for training data. While distant supervision has shown promise, it often results in noisy labels, which can significantly degrade the performance of neural NER models. Noisy labels can arise from various sources, including incomplete or outdated dictionaries, entities with multiple Possible labels, and entities that are not included in the dictionary. In this paper, we propose two neural models designed to handle noisy distant supervision from dictionaries. Our first model, built under the traditional sequence labeling framework, introduces a revised fuzzy CRF layer to handle tokens with multiple possible labels. This approach allows the model to effectively capture the uncertainty associated with noisy labels and improve its robustness to errors in the training data. However, after analyzing the nature of noisy labels in distant supervision, we propose a novel and more effective neural model, AutoNER, which goes beyond the traditional sequence labeling framework. AutoNER features a new Tie or Break scheme, which enables the model to dynamically adjust its label assignments based on the confidence of its predictions. This scheme allows AutoNER to effectively handle noisy labels and improve its overall performance. In addition to proposing these two neural models, we also investigate ways to refine distant supervision for better NER performance. We explore various strategies for improving the quality of the dictionary-based labels, including data augmentation, dictionary expansion, and label noise reduction. Our experiments demonstrate that these strategies can significantly enhance the performance of our proposed models. We evaluate our models on three benchmark datasets, including CoNLL-2003, OntoNotes 5.0, and WNUT-17. Our results show that AutoNER achieves the best performance when using only dictionaries with no additional human effort, outperforming state-of-the-art supervised benchmarks. Moreover, when combined with refined distant supervision, AutoNER delivers competitive results with supervised models trained on large amounts of manually labeled data.

Syntactic parsing is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), and it has been a subject of extensive research for several decades. The goal of syntactic parsing is to analyze the syntactic structure of a sentence, which is essential for many NLP applications, such as language translation, question answering, and text summarization. Over the years, various parsing algorithms have been developed, each with its strengths and weaknesses. One of the most widely used approaches is based on context-free dynamic programming algorithms, which work bottom-up on the entire sentence. These algorithms, such as the Cocke-Kasami-Younger (CKY) algorithm, are efficient and effective, but they have one major limitation: they only find a complete, fully connected parse at the very end of the parsing process. In contrast, human language understanding is known to be more incremental and left-to-right. Both subjective and experimental evidence suggest that people understand a sentence word-to-word as they go along, or close to it. For example, studies have shown that readers can quickly identify the syntactic structure of a sentence and make predictions about the upcoming words based on the context (Just and Carpenter, 1980). This incremental processing is thought to be essential for efficient and effective language comprehension. Motivated by these findings, we present a new syntactic parser that works left-to-right and top-down, thus maintaining a fully-connected parse tree for a few alternative parse hypotheses. Our parser is designed to operationalize the cognitive fact that people understand a sentence word-to-word as they go along. By keeping one or more fully connected syntactic trees, our parser can make predictions about the upcoming words and revise its parse hypothesis as new words are encountered. The key innovation of our parser is that it gives up dynamic programming in exchange for embracing a very large feature set. Dynamic programming is a powerful technique for parsing, but it requires the parser to consider all possible parse hypotheses and compute their probabilities. This can be computationally expensive and limits the parser's ability to incorporate a large number of features. In contrast, our parser uses a top-down approach, which allows it to focus on the most promising parse hypotheses and incorporate a much larger feature set. Our parser consists of two main components: a supertagger and a parser. The supertagger is responsible for identifying the syntactic category of each word, while the parser is responsible for building the parse tree.

The representation of text documents as numerical vectors is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in text classification, information retrieval, and topic modeling, among others. The goal of text representation is to capture the semantic meaning of a document in a way that can be efficiently processed by machine learning algorithms. Traditional methods for text representation, such as bag-of-words and term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF), have several limitations, including the inability to capture word semantics and the high dimensionality of the resulting vectors. In recent years, distributional paragraph vector representations, such as Paragraph Vector (PV) and Document Vector (DV), have gained popularity due to their ability to capture word semantics and context. These methods represent a document as a fixed-length vector, where each vector element captures a specific aspect of the document's meaning. However, current distributional paragraph vector representations have several shortcomings. Firstly, they rely on a fixed context window to define the context in which a word occurs, which can lead to loss of information and inability to capture long-range dependencies. Secondly, they fail to account for multiple semantic contexts in which a word can occur, resulting in poor representation of words with multiple meanings. To address these limitations, we propose a novel feature vector formation technique for documents, called Sparse Composite Document Vector (SCDV). SCDV overcomes the shortcomings of current distributional paragraph vector representations by clustering word embeddings to capture multiple semantic contexts in which words occur. The clustering process allows SCDV to identify words that have similar semantic meaning and group them together, resulting in a more informative and compact representation of the document. The SCDV method works as follows. Firstly, word embeddings are learned using a word2vec or glove model, which capture the semantic meaning of each word in a vector space. Secondly, the word embeddings are clustered using a soft clustering algorithm, such as k-means or hierarchical clustering, to identify groups of words that have similar semantic meaning. The clustering process results in a set of cluster centroids, each of which represents a specific semantic context. Thirdly, the cluster centroids are used to form document topic-vectors, which capture the semantic meaning of the document at a higher level of abstraction. The document topic-vectors are formed by taking a weighted sum of the cluster centroids, where the weights are learned during training. The resulting document topic-vectors are sparse, meaning that most of the elements are zero, which makes them efficient to store and process.

Named Entity (NE) recognition and alignment are crucial tasks in natural language processing, particularly in multilingual settings. The ability to accurately identify and link equivalent named entities across languages is essential for various applications, including machine translation, cross-lingual information retrieval, and question answering. However, the complexity of named entity translation and the diversity of linguistic and cultural contexts pose significant challenges to achieving high-quality NE alignment. In the context of bilingual named entity alignment, the task involves identifying named entities in two languages, such as Chinese and English, and establishing correspondences between them. The difficulty of this task lies in the fact that named entities can be translated in various ways, including semantic translation, phonetic translation, or a combination of both. Moreover, the translation approach often depends on the entity type, such as person, organization, or location. For instance, a person's name may be translated phonetically, while a location name may be translated semantically. Recent studies have shown that jointly recognizing and aligning bilingual named entities can lead to improved performance compared to pipelined approaches, where NE recognition and alignment are performed sequentially. However, these joint models often rely on simplistic features and do not fully capture the complexities of named entity translation and alignment. Specifically, they may not account for the entity type consistency constraint, which states that entities within an aligned pair should share the same type. To address these challenges, we propose an integrated model for jointly recognizing and aligning bilingual named entities between Chinese and English. Our approach is based on the following observations: (1) the translation approach for a given named entity depends greatly on its associated entity type; (2) entities within an aligned pair should share the same type; and (3) initially detected named entities can serve as anchors, providing certainty scores when selecting candidates. Our model incorporates a novel mapping type ratio feature, which represents the proportion of NE internal tokens that are semantically translated. This feature allows us to capture the translation approach used for each named entity and to distinguish between semantic and phonetic translations. Additionally, we enforce an entity type consistency constraint to ensure that entities within an aligned pair share the same type. This constraint is particularly important, as it helps to filter out incorrect alignments and to improve the overall quality of the aligned entity pairs. To further enhance the accuracy of our model, we utilize additional monolingual candidate certainty factors, which are based on the initially detected named entities.

Chinese word segmentation is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) for Chinese language, which is crucial for many downstream applications, such as language modeling, sentiment analysis, and machine translation. Unlike English, where words are separated by spaces, Chinese words are not explicitly separated, making word segmentation a challenging task. Traditional approaches to Chinese word segmentation rely heavily on hand-crafted features and rule-based methods, which require significant human effort and expertise. Recently, neural network-based approaches have gained popularity in Chinese word segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art performance. These models typically rely on character-level embeddings, which are learned from large amounts of text data. However, character-level embeddings may not capture the nuances of word-level semantics, as characters in different words can have different meanings. In this paper, we investigate the use of word-context character embeddings for Chinese word segmentation. The idea is to train character embeddings on a word-based context, similar to how dependency-context word embeddings are trained for neural parsers. By doing so, we aim to capture the word-level semantics of characters and improve the performance of neural word segmentation models. Our approach is simple yet effective. We start with a baseline segmentation model, which is a standard neural network-based approach to Chinese word segmentation. We then propose a novel method for training character embeddings on a word-based context, which we call word-context character embeddings. These embeddings are learned by predicting the surrounding words of a character, given the character itself. By training the embeddings in this way, we capture the word-level semantics of characters and provide a richer representation of the input text. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets for Chinese word segmentation, including the Penn Chinese Treebank (CTB) and the Microsoft Research (MSR) dataset. Our results show that the word-context character embeddings significantly improve the performance of the baseline segmentation model, achieving state-of-the-art results on both datasets. Furthermore, our approach outperforms tritraining baselines for leveraging auto-segmented data, which is a common approach to improving word segmentation performance. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we provide an overview of the baseline segmentation model and the word-context character embeddings approach. In Section 3, we describe the experimental setup and evaluation metrics used in our study. In Section 4, we present the results of our experiments and compare our approach to existing state-of-the-art methods.

The amount of unstructured data available on the web and other sources has been increasing exponentially over the past few decades. This has led to a growing need for automated methods to extract relevant information from such data, in order to enable effective search, retrieval, and utilization of the information. Traditional Information Extraction (IE) systems have been widely used for this purpose, but they have several limitations. They are typically designed to extract specific, pre-defined types of information, such as names, locations, and organizations, and require significant domain-specific knowledge and training data to achieve good performance. In contrast, Open Information Extraction (Open IE) systems aim to extract a wide range of relational information from unstructured data, without requiring any pre-defined schema or domain-specific knowledge. Open IE has been an active area of research over the past decade, with a wide range of approaches being proposed to address the challenges of extracting relational information from unstructured data. These approaches can be broadly categorized into two main types: sentence-level and corpus-level approaches. Sentence-level approaches focus on extracting relational information from individual sentences, using techniques such as pattern-based extraction, syntactic parsing, and semantic role labeling. Corpus-level approaches, on the other hand, aim to extract relational information from large collections of text, using techniques such as clustering, graph-based methods, and probabilistic models. One of the major challenges faced by Open IE systems is the lack of a clear definition of what constitutes "relational information". Unlike traditional IE systems, which extract specific, pre-defined types of information, Open IE systems need to be able to identify and extract a wide range of relationships between entities, without prior knowledge of the specific relationships that exist in the data. This makes it difficult to develop effective algorithms and evaluation metrics for Open IE systems. Another challenge faced by Open IE systems is the need to balance the trade-off between precision and recall. On the one hand, the system needs to be able to extract as much relational information as possible from the data, in order to maximize recall. On the other hand, the system needs to ensure that the extracted information is accurate and reliable, in order to maximize precision. This trade-off is particularly challenging in Open IE, where the lack of a clear definition of what constitutes "relational information" makes it difficult to develop effective algorithms that can achieve high precision and recall.

With the rapid growth of the web, search engines have become an essential tool for people to access information. However, the ambiguity and variability of natural language make it challenging for search engines to understand the intent behind a user's query. One effective way to improve the search engine's understanding of user intent is to leverage paraphrase queries, which are alternative ways of expressing the same search intent. Paraphrase queries can help search engines to capture the nuances of user intent, improve query suggestion, and enhance overall search experience. Search log sessions, which contain a sequence of queries submitted by a user during a search task, are a rich source of paraphrase queries. Users often reformulate their queries during a search session, providing a large number of paraphrases that can be used to improve search engines. However, it is a big challenge to distinguish paraphrases from simply related queries in the sessions. Simply related queries are queries that are related to the same topic or domain but do not necessarily express the same search intent. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that makes innovative use of user behavior information embodied in query sessions. Our approach learns paraphrase patterns from search log sessions using a classification framework, which exploits three types of user behavior features besides conventional features. The user behavior features we use include: 1. Query reformulation features: These features capture the ways in which users reformulate their queries during a search session. For example, we use features such as the number of queries submitted, the time spent on each query, and the similarity between consecutive queries. 2. Click-through features: These features capture the ways in which users interact with search results. For example, we use features such as the number of clicks on search results, the time spent on each result, and the similarity between clicked results. 3. Session structure features: These features capture the overall structure of the search session. For example, we use features such as the number of queries in the session, the duration of the session, and the similarity between queries submitted at different times. We evaluate our method using a query log of a commercial search engine, which contains millions of search sessions. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, especially the significant contribution of the user behavior features. We extract over 250,000 pairs of paraphrase patterns from the used search log, with a precision over 76%.

Word representation learning has been a crucial component in many natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including text classification, sentiment analysis, and machine translation. The distributional hypothesis in linguistics, which states that words that are used and occur in the same contexts tend to possess similar meanings, has been the foundation of most word representation learning methods. This hypothesis has led to the development of various word embedding algorithms, such as Word2Vec and GloVe, which have achieved impressive results in many NLP tasks. However, these methods have a significant limitation when it comes to capturing the emotional aspects of words. Emotionally dissimilar words, such as "happy" and "sad", which occur in similar contexts, are often represented as having similar meanings, while emotionally similar words, such as "happy" and "joy", are not necessarily close to each other in the vector space. This complication can lead to undesirable outcomes in predictive tasks related to affect, such as emotion classification and emotion similarity. For instance, in emotion classification tasks, words with similar emotional connotations, such as "happy" and "delighted", should be represented in a way that captures their emotional similarity. However, using traditional word embedding methods, these words may not be close to each other in the vector space, especially if they occur in different contexts. Similarly, in emotion similarity tasks, words with opposite emotional connotations, such as "happy" and "sad", should be represented in a way that captures their emotional dissimilarity. However, traditional word embedding methods may represent these words as having similar meanings, simply because they occur in similar contexts. To address this limitation, we propose a novel method of obtaining emotion-enriched word representations, which projects emotionally similar words into neighboring spaces and emotionally dissimilar ones far apart. Our approach leverages distant supervision to automatically obtain a large training dataset of text documents, which are annotated with emotional labels. We use two recurrent neural network (RNN) architectures to learn the emotion-enriched representations. The first RNN architecture is used to model the emotional context of each word, while the second RNN architecture is used to model the emotional similarity between words. Our method has several advantages over traditional word embedding methods. First, it captures the emotional aspects of words, which is essential for tasks related to affect. Second, it uses distant supervision to automatically obtain a large training dataset, which reduces the need for manual annotation. Third, it uses RNN architectures to model the emotional context and similarity between words, which can capture complex emotional relationships.

Morphological segmentation, the process of dividing words into their constituent morphemes, is a crucial component of many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. It is particularly important for languages with rich morphology, where words can be composed of multiple prefixes, roots, and suffixes. Despite its importance, morphological segmentation remains a challenging task, particularly for languages with limited resources, where annotated datasets may not be available. Morfessor is a family of methods for learning morphological segmentations of words based on unannotated data. The Morfessor approach has been successfully applied to a variety of languages, including English, Finnish, and Turkish. The key idea behind Morfessor is to use a statistical model to identify the most likely morphological segmentation of a word, based on the patterns and structures observed in a large corpus of unannotated text. In this paper, we introduce a new variant of Morfessor, FlatCat, which applies a hidden Markov model (HMM) structure to the task of morphological segmentation. The FlatCat model builds on previous work on Morfessor, sharing model components with the popular Morfessor Baseline and Categories-MAP variants. The use of an HMM structure allows FlatCat to model the sequential dependencies between morphemes in a word, and to capture the probabilistic relationships between different morphological segments. Our experiments show that while unsupervised FlatCat does not reach the accuracy of Categories-MAP, with semi-supervised learning it provides state-of-the-art results in the Morpho Challenge 2010 tasks for English, Finnish, and Turkish. The Morpho Challenge is a benchmark evaluation framework for morphological segmentation systems, and the 2010 tasks provide a comprehensive testbed for evaluating the performance of different systems on a variety of languages and datasets. The FlatCat model is based on a probabilistic framework, where the goal is to find the most likely sequence of morphemes that generates a given word. The model consists of a set of states, each representing a morpheme, and a set of transitions between these states, which represent the probabilities of moving from one morpheme to another. The model is trained on a large corpus of unannotated text, where the goal is to find the most likely state sequence that generates each word in the corpus. The use of an HMM structure in FlatCat provides several advantages over previous Morfessor variants. First, it allows the model to capture the sequential dependencies between morphemes in a word, which is particularly important for languages with complex morphology.

The acquisition of relational patterns from text has been a central task in natural language processing (NLP) and information extraction (IE) for several decades. Relational patterns are crucial for extracting binary relations between entities, such as "person born-in city" or "organization founded-by person". These patterns are essential for populating knowledge bases, question answering, and text summarization, among other applications. However, the sheer variability of natural language makes it challenging to identify and organize these patterns in a scalable and efficient manner. Existing approaches to pattern acquisition have relied on hand-crafted rules, supervised learning, or unsupervised methods. Hand-crafted rules are time-consuming to create and often limited in coverage, while supervised learning requires large amounts of labeled training data. Unsupervised methods, such as those based on clustering or frequent itemset mining, can discover patterns automatically but often lack semantic interpretability. To address these challenges, we present PATTY, a large resource for textual patterns that denote binary relations between entities. PATTY is built on a novel combination of efficient algorithms for frequent itemset mining and the rich type system and entity population of large knowledge bases. The patterns in PATTY are semantically typed, meaning that each pattern is associated with a specific relation type, such as "born-in" or "founded-by". Additionally, the patterns are organized into a subsumption taxonomy, which allows for efficient navigation and querying of the pattern space. The PATTY system consists of three main components: (1) a pattern mining algorithm that extracts frequent patterns from a large corpus of text, (2) a semantic typing module that assigns relation types to each pattern, and (3) a taxonomy construction module that organizes the patterns into a subsumption hierarchy. The pattern mining algorithm is based on a variant of the well-known Apriori algorithm, which is optimized for efficiency and scalability. The semantic typing module leverages the rich type system of large knowledge bases, such as YAGO or Freebase, to assign relation types to each pattern. The taxonomy construction module uses a combination of lexical and semantic similarity measures to organize the patterns into a subsumption hierarchy. The PATTY taxonomy comprises 350,569 pattern synsets, each representing a unique relational pattern. To evaluate the accuracy of the patterns, we conducted a random-sampling-based evaluation, which showed a pattern accuracy of 84.7%. This means that approximately 85% of the patterns in PATTY are correct and useful for extracting binary relations.

Estimating word similarities from text is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in text classification, clustering, information retrieval, and language modeling, among others. Word similarities are typically estimated by analyzing the co-occurrence patterns of words in large corpora. The underlying idea is that words that appear in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings. One popular approach to estimating word similarities is to use word embeddings, which represent words as vectors in a high-dimensional space such that semantically similar words are mapped to nearby points. Word embeddings have been shown to capture nuanced aspects of word meaning and have achieved state-of-the-art results in a variety of NLP tasks. However, traditional word embedding methods, such as Word2Vec and GloVe, require large amounts of memory and computational resources to process large corpora. Moreover, they are often designed to work with static, pre-processed datasets, which can be limiting in scenarios where data is streaming in or is too large to fit in memory. Recently, there has been a growing interest in developing methods that can efficiently process streams of text data, such as social media posts, news articles, and online forums. These methods, often referred to as "streaming" or "online" methods, aim to process data in a single pass, without requiring large amounts of memory or computational resources. In this paper, we propose a fast and lightweight method for estimating word similarities from streams of text data. Our approach is based on explicitly counting second-order co-occurrences, which capture the similarity between words in terms of their co-occurrence patterns with other words. We observe that words that are highly correlated with respect to these counts are also highly similar with respect to first-order co-occurrences, which capture the similarity between words in terms of their co-occurrence patterns with each other. By using buffers of co-occurred words per word to count second-order co-occurrences, we can estimate similarities in a single pass over the data without having to perform prohibitively expensive similarity calculations. Our approach has several advantages over traditional word embedding methods. First, it is highly scalable and can handle large volumes of data without requiring significant computational resources. Second, it converges rapidly, allowing for accurate estimates of word similarities to be obtained from relatively small amounts of data. Third, it behaves robustly under parameter changes, making it easy to tune and optimize.

Tree-to-string translation is a machine translation framework that converts a source tree to a target string. This framework has been widely used in statistical machine translation due to its ability to effectively model the syntactic structure of the source language and generate fluent target language strings. In tree-to-string translation, the source tree is typically represented as a parse tree, which is a hierarchical representation of the syntactic structure of the source sentence. The goal of the translation system is to map this source tree to a target string, which is the translated sentence in the target language. One of the key challenges in tree-to-string translation is how to effectively model the syntactic structure of the source language and generate fluent target language strings. Early work in tree-to-string translation used simple tree substitution grammar (TSG) rules, which allow for the substitution of a subtree in the source tree with a string in the target language. However, these rules are limited in their ability to model complex syntactic structures and generate fluent target language strings. To address this limitation, recent work has focused on using more powerful grammatical formalisms, such as synchronous tree adjoining grammars (TAG). TAG is a formalism that allows for the manipulation of trees using a set of operations, including substitution, adjunction, and wrapping. Synchronous TAG is an extension of TAG that allows for the simultaneous manipulation of two trees, one for the source language and one for the target language. This formalism has been shown to be effective in modeling complex syntactic structures and generating fluent target language strings. In this paper, we introduce synchronous TAG into tree-to-string translation, which converts a source tree to a target string. Our approach uses a rule extraction algorithm that directly learns tree-to-string rules from aligned Treebank-style trees, without reconstructing TAG derivations explicitly. This approach allows for the effective modeling of complex syntactic structures and the generation of fluent target language strings. One of the key advantages of our approach is that it does not require the explicit reconstruction of TAG derivations. This makes it possible to use TAG in a tree-to-string translation system without incurring a significant increase in computational cost. In fact, our experiments show that the decoder runs less than 2 times slower than the baseline system, which only allows for tree substitution. We evaluate our approach on the NIST Chinese-English test sets, which are a standard benchmark for machine translation systems.

The increasing availability of electronic medical records (EMRs) has created new opportunities for natural language processing (NLP) to improve healthcare outcomes. One key application of NLP in this domain is question answering (QA), where systems aim to accurately extract relevant information from clinical notes to answer specific clinical questions. However, the development of large-scale QA datasets for EMRs has been hindered by the lack of annotated data, which is essential for training and evaluating QA models. To address this challenge, we propose a novel methodology for generating domain-specific large-scale QA datasets by re-purposing existing annotations for other NLP tasks. Our approach leverages the fact that many NLP tasks, such as named entity recognition, relation extraction, and sentiment analysis, require annotated datasets that can be repurposed for QA. By utilizing these existing annotations, we can create large-scale QA datasets without the need for additional manual annotation, which is often time-consuming and expensive. In this paper, we demonstrate an instance of this methodology by generating a large-scale QA dataset for EMRs, which we call emrQA. We leverage existing expert annotations on clinical notes from the community shared i2b2 datasets, which have been annotated for various NLP tasks such as named entity recognition, relation extraction, and cohort selection. Our methodology involves automatically generating questions and their corresponding logical forms and answers from these annotated datasets. The resulting emrQA corpus consists of over 1 million questions-logical form pairs and 400,000+ question-answer evidence pairs. To the best of our knowledge, this is the largest QA dataset for EMRs to date, providing a valuable resource for the development and evaluation of QA systems in this domain. We characterize the dataset by analyzing its statistical properties, such as question types, answer distributions, and entity recognition performance. To explore the learning potential of emrQA, we train baseline models for two key QA tasks: question to logical form mapping and question to answer mapping. For question to logical form mapping, we evaluate the performance of sequence-to-sequence models, such as encoder-decoder architectures, in generating logical forms from questions. For question to answer mapping, we evaluate the performance of machine comprehension models, such as those based on attention mechanisms, in extracting answers from clinical notes given questions. Our experimental results show that the emrQA dataset provides a challenging yet valuable benchmark for QA systems in the EMR domain. The baseline models achieve reasonable performance on both tasks, but there is still significant room for improvement, highlighting the need for further research in this area.

Semantic role labeling (SRL) is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) that aims to identify the predicate-argument structure of a sentence, which is essential for understanding the meaning of a sentence. The task involves recognizing the relationships between a predicate (e.g., a verb) and its arguments (e.g., entities participating in the action described by the predicate). For instance, in the sentence "The cat chased the mouse", the verb "chased" is the predicate, and "the cat" and "the mouse" are its arguments, playing the roles of "agent" and "patient", respectively. Previous studies have demonstrated that syntactic information plays a vital role in SRL, as it provides a way to capture the relationships between words in a sentence. The syntactic structure of a sentence, including phrase structure and dependency relations, can help to identify the arguments of a predicate and their corresponding roles. For example, the subject of a sentence is more likely to be the agent of a verb, while the object is more likely to be the patient. Many traditional SRL systems rely heavily on syntactic features, such as part-of-speech tags, named entity recognition, and parse trees, to perform argument identification and role labeling. However, with the advent of deep learning techniques, some recent neural SRL models have achieved impressive performance without explicitly incorporating syntactic information into their architectures. These models often rely on word embeddings, such as Word2Vec or GloVe, and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or transformers to learn contextualized representations of words in a sentence. While these models have shown promising results, it is unclear whether they truly capture the underlying syntactic structure of a sentence or simply memorize patterns in the training data. In this paper, we aim to quantify the importance of syntactic information to dependency SRL in a deep learning framework. We propose an enhanced argument labeling model that effectively exploits syntactic information, along with an extended k-order argument pruning algorithm to improve the efficiency of the model. Our model achieves state-of-the-art results on the CoNLL-2008 and 2009 benchmarks for both English and Chinese, demonstrating the quantitative significance of syntax to neural SRL. We also conduct a thorough empirical survey over existing models to investigate the role of syntax in SRL and provide insights into the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review the related work on SRL, including traditional syntactic-based approaches and recent neural models.

Sentiment analysis is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in fields such as marketing, customer service, and social media monitoring. The goal of sentiment analysis is to determine the emotional tone or attitude conveyed by a piece of text, such as a sentence or a document. Traditional approaches to sentiment analysis have relied on manual feature engineering, using techniques such as bag-of-words or sentiment lexicons to extract relevant features from text data. However, these approaches have several limitations, including the need for large amounts of labeled training data and the difficulty of capturing nuanced or context-dependent sentiment expressions. In recent years, deep learning techniques have shown great promise for sentiment analysis tasks. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been used to learn vector space representations of text data, which can be used for sentiment classification and other NLP tasks. However, these models often require large amounts of labeled training data to achieve good performance, which can be a limitation in many real-world applications. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel machine learning framework based on semi-supervised recursive autoencoders (SSRA) for sentence-level prediction of sentiment label distributions. Our method learns vector space representations for multi-word phrases, which can be used to predict sentiment labels and capture nuanced sentiment expressions. The key innovation of our approach is the use of a recursive autoencoder architecture, which allows us to learn hierarchical representations of text data and capture long-range dependencies between words and phrases. Our SSRA model consists of two main components: a recursive autoencoder and a sentiment prediction module. The recursive autoencoder is used to learn vector space representations of text data, while the sentiment prediction module is used to predict sentiment labels based on these representations. We train the model using a combination of labeled and unlabeled data, which allows us to leverage the large amounts of unlabeled text data available in many applications. We evaluate our SSRA model on several benchmark datasets, including movie reviews and product reviews. Our results show that our model outperforms several state-of-the-art approaches, including those based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs). We also evaluate our model on a new dataset based on confessions from the experience project, which consists of personal user stories annotated with multiple labels that form a multinomial distribution.

The advent of globalization and the proliferation of the internet have led to an increased need for effective communication across linguistic and cultural boundaries. Machine translation and cross-lingual information retrieval systems have become essential tools in facilitating this communication, and bilingual lexicons are a crucial component of these systems. A bilingual lexicon is a dictionary that maps words or phrases from one language to their equivalent translations in another language. However, the manual construction of bilingual lexicons is a time-consuming and labor-intensive process that requires strong expertise in both languages involved. Furthermore, the cost of creating and maintaining large-scale bilingual lexicons can be prohibitively expensive. As a result, researchers have been exploring automatic methods for constructing bilingual lexicons. These methods typically rely on parallel corpora, which are collections of texts and their translations in two or more languages. However, parallel corpora are often limited to a small number of language pairs, and the quality of the automatically constructed lexicons often lags behind that of manually curated ones. Moreover, the scarcity of parallel corpora for many language pairs, especially for low-resource languages, hinders the development of machine translation and cross-lingual information retrieval systems for these languages. In recent years, Wikipedia has emerged as a valuable resource for natural language processing tasks, including bilingual lexicon construction. Wikipedia is a massively multilingual encyclopedia that contains a vast amount of text in many languages, making it an attractive source of background knowledge for constructing bilingual lexicons. Each Wikipedia article is associated with a specific domain or topic, and the articles are often translated into multiple languages. This makes it possible to extract domain-specific terminology and phrases from Wikipedia articles and use them to construct bilingual lexicons. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to constructing specialized domain bilingual lexicons using large-scale background knowledge from Wikipedia. Our approach involves three main steps: domain extraction, domain linking, and lexicon construction. First, we extract domains from Wikipedia articles in each language using a combination of natural language processing techniques and Wikipedia's category system. Then, we link the extracted domains between languages using Wikipedia's interlanguage links, which connect articles on the same topic across different languages. Finally, we construct generic translation dictionaries for each domain by leveraging the linked articles and extracting terminology and phrases that are relevant to the domain. We test our approach on four specialized domains ( medicine, law, sports, and technology) and compare it to three state-of-the-art approaches using two language pairs: French-English and Romanian-English.

The rise of online media has led to a proliferation of political blogs, where individuals can express their opinions and engage in discussions with others. These blogs provide a unique window into the thoughts and feelings of the public, and can be a valuable resource for understanding political discourse. However, the sheer volume of data generated by these blogs can be overwhelming, making it difficult to extract meaningful insights. In recent years, topic models have emerged as a powerful tool for analyzing large collections of text data. These models are based on the idea that documents can be represented as mixtures of underlying topics, where each topic is characterized by a distribution over words. By applying topic models to political blog data, we can gain a deeper understanding of the underlying themes and trends that shape online political discourse. In this paper, we extend Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), a popular topic model, to capture different characteristics of online political blog data. Our models jointly describe the generation of primary documents (posts) as well as the authorship and, optionally, the contents of the blog community's verbal reactions to each post (comments). This allows us to model the relationships between posts and comments, and to capture the ways in which different authors and topics interact with one another. One of the key challenges in modeling online political blog data is capturing the diversity of perspectives and opinions that are present in these discussions. Traditional topic models, such as LDA, are limited in their ability to capture this diversity, as they assume that each document can be represented as a mixture of a fixed set of topics. In contrast, our models allow for a more nuanced representation of the data, where each post and comment can be associated with a unique set of topics and authors. We evaluate our model on a novel comment prediction task, where the models are used to predict which blog users will leave comments on a given post. This task is challenging, as it requires the model to capture the complex relationships between posts, authors, and topics. Our results show that our model is able to accurately predict which users will comment on a given post, and that it outperforms baseline models that do not capture the same level of complexity. In addition to its quantitative performance, our model also provides a number of qualitative insights into the nature of online political discourse.

Gender classification is a fundamental task in natural language processing and social network analysis, with various applications such as personalized marketing, recommender systems, and demographic analysis. The goal of gender classification is to determine the gender of an individual based on their written text, social media profiles, or other online activities. Supervised learning approaches have been widely used for gender classification, which require a large amount of labeled data to achieve good performance. However, labeled data is often limited, expensive, and time-consuming to obtain, while unlabeled data is abundant and can be easily collected. This limitation motivates the use of semi-supervised learning for gender classification, which aims to improve the performance by exploring the knowledge in both labeled and unlabeled data. Semi-supervised learning has been successfully applied to various natural language processing tasks, such as text classification, sentiment analysis, and machine translation. The key idea of semi-supervised learning is to leverage the unlabeled data to improve the model's performance on the labeled data. There are several semi-supervised learning approaches, including self-training, co-training, and graph-based methods. Self-training involves training a model on the labeled data and then using the model to predict the labels of the unlabeled data. Co-training involves training two models on different views of the data and then using the models to predict the labels of the unlabeled data. Graph-based methods involve representing the data as a graph and then using graph-based algorithms to propagate the labels from the labeled data to the unlabeled data. In this paper, we propose a semi-supervised approach to gender classification by leveraging textual features and a specific kind of indirect links among the users, which we call "same-interest" links. Same-interest links refer to the links between users who have similar interests, such as following the same topics or hashtags on social media. These links can provide valuable information for gender classification, as users with similar interests are more likely to have the same gender. For example, users who follow fashion or beauty topics are more likely to be female, while users who follow sports or technology topics are more likely to be male. To model both the textual and the same-interest link information, we propose a factor graph, namely Textual and Social Factor Graph (TSFG). A factor graph is a probabilistic graphical model that can represent the relationships between variables in a flexible and efficient way.

Sentiment classification is a crucial task in natural language processing (NLP), which aims to determine the emotional tone or attitude conveyed by a piece of text, such as a review or a comment. With the rapid growth of online review platforms, sentiment classification has become increasingly important for businesses and individuals to understand customer opinions and make informed decisions. However, one of the significant challenges in sentiment classification is the cold-start problem, which occurs when a new user or product has only a limited number of reviews, making it difficult to accurately predict their sentiment. Traditional sentiment classification models rely heavily on the content of the text itself, ignoring the importance of user and product information. However, user and product information can provide valuable context for understanding the sentiment expressed in a review. For example, a review from a user who has consistently written positive reviews in the past is more likely to be positive, even if the content of the review is neutral or negative. Similarly, a review for a product that has received overwhelmingly positive reviews from other users is more likely to be positive, even if the content of the review is negative. To address the cold-start problem, several models have been proposed that incorporate user and product information into the sentiment classification task. These models typically use various techniques, such as matrix factorization or neural networks, to learn user and product embeddings that capture their sentiment preferences. However, these models often rely on a large amount of training data and can be computationally expensive to train, which can be a limitation in practice. In this paper, we propose a novel model called Hybrid Contextualized Sentiment Classifier (HCSC), which is designed to address the cold-start problem in sentiment classification. HCSC consists of two modules: a fast word encoder that returns word vectors embedded with short and long-range dependency features, and a Cold-Start Aware Attention (CSAA) mechanism that considers the existence of the cold-start problem when attentively pooling the encoded word vectors. The key innovation of HCSC is the introduction of shared vectors that are constructed from similar users or products, which are used when the original distinct vectors do not have sufficient information (i.e., cold-start). This is decided by a frequency-guided selective gate vector. The use of shared vectors in HCSC is motivated by the idea that similar users or products are likely to have similar sentiment preferences.

Minimum Error Rate Training (MERT) is a widely used optimization technique in Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications such as machine translation, speech recognition, and summarization. The goal of MERT is to find the optimal set of model parameters that minimize the error rate of a system, where the error rate is typically measured using evaluation metrics such as BLEU, Word Error Rate (WER), or ROUGE. However, the search space of model parameters is often highly non-convex, making it challenging to find the global optimum using traditional optimization techniques. Conventional MERT algorithms, such as the Och algorithm (Och, 2003), rely on heuristic search strategies to find the optimal model parameters. These algorithms typically start with an initial set of parameters and iteratively update them using a local search strategy, such as gradient descent or powell's method. However, these algorithms are prone to getting stuck in local optima, especially when the search space is highly non-convex. In this paper, we present LP-MERT, an exact search algorithm for minimum error rate training that reaches the global optimum using a series of reductions to linear programming. LP-MERT takes as input a set of N-best lists produced from S input sentences and finds a linear model that is globally optimal with respect to this set. The algorithm is based on the observation that the error rate of a system can be represented as a linear function of the model parameters, and that the optimal model parameters can be found by solving a linear programming problem. The LP-MERT algorithm works as follows. First, we create a set of constraints, one for each sentence in the tuning set, that represent the error rate of the system for a given set of model parameters. Each constraint is a linear function of the model parameters and represents the difference between the predicted output and the reference output for a given sentence. We then combine these constraints into a single linear programming problem, which we solve using a linear programming solver. The resulting algorithm is polynomial in N, the number of N-best lists, and in the size of the model, but exponential in S, the number of sentences in the tuning set. This means that LP-MERT can be used to optimize models with thousands of parameters, but may not be practical for large tuning sets. To address this limitation, we present two extensions of LP-MERT that allow us to scale to reasonably large tuning sets.

The proliferation of social media platforms such as Twitter has led to a tremendous amount of user-generated content being produced every day. Twitter, with its 330 million monthly active users, is a rich source of real-time information on various topics, including news, events, and trends. However, the sheer volume and velocity of Twitter data make it challenging to analyze and summarize. Traditional text summarization techniques, which rely on extracting the most important sentences or phrases from a document, are not well-suited for Twitter data due to its short and informal nature. Moreover, Twitter posts often contain noise, such as hashtags, URLs, and mentions, which can make it difficult to identify the most relevant and meaningful content. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach to summarizing Twitter content by extracting topical keyphrases. Keyphrases are phrases that capture the main idea or topic of a document, and extracting them can provide a concise and meaningful summary of the content. Topical keyphrases, in particular, are keyphrases that are relevant to a specific topic or theme, making them an ideal way to summarize Twitter content, which is often centered around specific topics or events. Several approaches have been proposed for keyphrase extraction, including unsupervised methods such as TextRank and RAKE, and supervised methods such as Keyphrase Extraction using Graph-based Methods and Deep Learning-based Methods. However, these approaches have several limitations when applied to Twitter data. Firstly, they often rely on part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition, which can be noisy and inaccurate for Twitter data due to its informal nature. Secondly, they often use a fixed window size to extract keyphrases, which can lead to missing important keyphrases that are longer or shorter than the fixed window size. Finally, they often do not consider the context and relevance of the keyphrases, which is crucial for Twitter data where the same keyphrase can have different meanings depending on the context. To overcome these limitations, we propose a context-sensitive topical PageRank method for keyword ranking and a probabilistic scoring function that considers both relevance and interestingness of keyphrases for keyphrase ranking. Our approach is designed specifically for Twitter data and takes into account the unique characteristics of Twitter posts, such as the use of hashtags, URLs, and mentions. We also propose a novel evaluation metric that assesses the quality of the extracted keyphrases in terms of their relevance, interestingness, and coverage of the topic.

The acquisition of language by children is a complex and multifaceted process, involving the simultaneous learning of various levels of linguistic structure, including phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics. Despite the intuitive notion that these levels of structure are interrelated and influence one another, most existing models of language acquisition have focused on a single level of structure, implicitly assuming a sequential learning process. However, this assumption is not supported by empirical evidence, which suggests that children learn multiple levels of linguistic structure concurrently. Morphology and syntax are two fundamental levels of linguistic structure that are closely intertwined. Morphology refers to the internal structure of words and how they are formed from smaller units such as roots and affixes, while syntax refers to the rules governing how words are combined to form sentences. In language acquisition, children must learn to segment words into their constituent morphemes and to recognize the syntactic categories of words, such as noun, verb, and adjective. Recently, there has been a growing interest in developing models that can learn multiple levels of linguistic structure simultaneously. These models are often referred to as "joint" or "multi-task" models, and they have been shown to be effective in a variety of natural language processing tasks, including language modeling, machine translation, and speech recognition. In this paper, we present a joint model of morphological and syntactic learning, which combines two well-known models for the individual tasks. Our model is designed to learn from child-directed speech, which is a type of language that is typically used by caregivers to communicate with young children. Child-directed speech is characterized by its simplicity, clarity, and repetitiveness, making it an ideal data source for language acquisition research. We test our joint model on child-directed utterances in English and Spanish, two languages that differ significantly in their morphological complexity. English is a relatively morphologically poor language, with a simple system of inflectional morphology, while Spanish is a morphologically richer language, with a more complex system of inflectional and derivational morphology. Our results show that the joint model outperforms single-task baselines in both languages, but the benefits of joint learning are more pronounced in certain tasks and languages. In English, the joint model improves morphological segmentation, suggesting that syntactic information can help to disambiguate morphological boundaries. In Spanish, the joint model leads to better syntactic categorization, suggesting that morphological information can help to inform syntactic category assignment.

Coreference resolution is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) that involves identifying all expressions in a document that refer to the same entity. It is a crucial component in many NLP applications, such as information extraction, question answering, and text summarization. Over the years, a wide range of approaches have been proposed to tackle this problem, including rule-based systems, machine learning-based models, and hybrid approaches. Despite the significant progress made in this area, coreference resolution remains a challenging task, particularly in cases where the relationships between entities are complex or ambiguous. One of the key challenges in coreference resolution is the evaluation metric used to measure the performance of a system. The most commonly used metrics for coreference resolution are the MUC metric (Vilain et al., 1995) and the B-CUBED metric (Bagga and Baldwin, 1998). These metrics are designed to capture the quality of a coreference resolution system's output, but they are not always aligned with the objective function used in traditional supervised machine learning algorithms. As a result, a system that is optimized to minimize classification errors on the training instances may not necessarily achieve the best performance on the evaluation metric. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to coreference resolution that directly optimizes the evaluation metric score on the training corpus during training. Our approach combines instance weighting and beam search to maximize the metric score, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on several standard benchmark corpora. The key insight behind our approach is that the evaluation metric score can be decomposed into a sum of scores for each individual coreference link. By assigning weights to each instance based on its contribution to the overall metric score, we can focus the training process on the most informative instances and maximize the overall performance of the system. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review the background and related work on coreference resolution and evaluation metrics. In Section 3, we present our proposed approach, including the instance weighting and beam search algorithms. In Section 4, we describe our experimental setup and evaluate our approach on several benchmark corpora. Finally, in Section 5, we conclude and discuss future directions for this work. Coreference resolution has been a long-standing challenge in NLP, and a wide range of approaches have been proposed to tackle this problem. Early work on coreference resolution focused on rule-based systems, which relied on hand-crafted rules and heuristics to identify coreference relationships (Hobbs, 1978; Baldwin, 1997).

Human sentence processing is a complex and multi-faceted phenomenon that has been studied extensively in the fields of psycholinguistics, linguistics, and cognitive science. One of the key challenges in understanding human sentence processing is to develop a model that can accurately predict how humans process and comprehend sentences. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in developing computational models of sentence processing that can simulate human-like behavior and provide insights into the cognitive mechanisms underlying language comprehension. One important aspect of sentence processing is the role of discourse predictions, which refer to the expectations and inferences that readers or listeners make about the meaning and structure of a sentence based on the context in which it is presented. Discourse predictions play a crucial role in shaping the way we process and comprehend sentences, and they have been shown to influence a range of linguistic phenomena, including syntactic parsing, semantic interpretation, and pragmatic inference. In this paper, we introduce a psycholinguistic model of sentence processing that combines a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) noun phrase chunker with a co-reference classifier. Both models are fully incremental and generative, which means that they can process sentences in a word-by-word manner and generate probabilities for each word based on the linguistic structure of the sentence. This allows us to compute the information-theoretic measure of surprisal, which is known to correlate with human processing effort. Surprisal is a measure of the amount of information that a word or phrase conveys in a given context, and it has been shown to be a strong predictor of human reading times and processing difficulty. By using a combination of HMM and co-reference classification, our model is able to capture a range of linguistic phenomena that influence discourse predictions, including syntactic structure, semantic meaning, and co-referential relationships between entities. We evaluate our model on the Dundee corpus of eye-movement data, which consists of a large collection of sentences that have been annotated with eye-tracking data from human readers. Our results show that our model achieves a better fit with human reading times than a syntax-only model that does not have access to co-reference information. This suggests that our model is able to capture the role of discourse predictions in shaping human sentence processing, and that it provides a more accurate and comprehensive account of the cognitive mechanisms underlying language comprehension.

The rapid growth of digital communication has led to an increased demand for machine translation (MT) systems that can accurately translate informal text, such as dialogues. However, research in statistical machine translation (SMT) has largely focused on formal translation tasks, leaving the challenge of translating informal text relatively unexplored. Translating dialogues is particularly difficult due to their unique characteristics, such as colloquial language, context-dependent expressions, and speaker-specific traits. These aspects can significantly impact the quality of machine-translated text, and understanding their effects is essential for developing more accurate and nuanced MT systems. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in exploring the role of conversational aspects in SMT. For instance, previous studies have investigated the impact of dialogue structure, speaker roles, and emotions on translation quality. However, these studies have been limited in scope, and a comprehensive analysis of the effect of conversational aspects on SMT quality is still lacking. Furthermore, the majority of existing research has focused on formal dialogue genres, such as parliamentary debates or court proceedings, while the translation of fictional dialogues has received relatively little attention. Fictional dialogues, such as those found in movies or literature, pose a unique challenge for MT systems. They often involve complex characters, nuanced language, and context-dependent expressions, which can be difficult to translate accurately. Moreover, fictional dialogues frequently include informal language, colloquialisms, and cultural references that may not be easily translatable. To address these challenges, it is essential to develop MT systems that can effectively capture the conversational aspects of fictional dialogues and adapt to their unique characteristics. In this paper, we investigate the effect of dialogue acts, speakers, gender, and text register on SMT quality when translating fictional dialogues. We create and release a corpus of multilingual movie dialogues annotated with these four dialogue-specific aspects, which provides a valuable resource for researchers and developers of MT systems. Our analysis reveals that the translation performance of SMT systems can vary significantly depending on the category of dialogue act, speaker, gender, and text register. For example, we find that translations of dialogue acts that involve imperatives or questions tend to be less accurate than those that involve statements. Similarly, male speakers are found to be harder to translate than female speakers, and translations of text with a formal register tend to be more accurate than those with an informal register. Our findings have significant implications for the development of MT systems for fictional dialogues.

Machine translation (MT) has made significant progress in recent years, with the development of phrase-based statistical MT systems (Koehn et al., 2003;Lopez, 2008). These systems rely on a combination of translation models, language models, and decoding algorithms to produce high-quality translations. One of the key challenges in MT is the need for efficient and accurate syntactic analysis of the input sentence. Traditional syntactic parsing approaches, such as context-free grammar parsing, have a time complexity of O(n^3), where n is the length of the sentence. This can be a significant bottleneck in MT decoding, particularly for long sentences or large-scale translation tasks. Recently, McDonald et al. (2005b) proposed a novel approach to dependency parsing, which formalizes the parsing problem as a maximum spanning tree (MST) problem. This approach has a time complexity of O(n^2), making it much more efficient than traditional parsing approaches. The MST parser works by representing the sentence as a graph, where each node corresponds to a word in the sentence, and each edge corresponds to a potential dependency relation between two words. The parser then selects the maximum spanning tree of this graph, which corresponds to the most likely dependency parse of the sentence. The MST parsing approach has been shown to be highly effective for dependency parsing, particularly for languages with free word order (McDonald et al., 2005b). It has also been shown to be competitive with more traditional cubic-time dependency parsing approaches, such as those based on probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs) (Charniak, 2000). However, the application of MST parsing to machine translation has not been fully explored. In this paper, we apply the MST parsing approach to machine translation, and describe how it can be integrated into a phrase-based decoder to compute dependency language model scores. Our approach involves the following steps: (1) parsing the input sentence using the MST parser to produce a dependency parse tree; (2) using the dependency parse tree to compute a dependency language model score for each possible translation; and (3) incorporating the dependency language model score into the phrase-based decoder to produce the final translation. We evaluate our approach on five NIST Chinese-English evaluation test sets, using a state-of-the-art phrase-based MT system as the baseline. Our results show that augmenting the baseline system with the dependency language model leads to significant improvements in translation quality, as measured by TER (0.92%) and BLEU (0.45%) scores.

Transliteration, the process of converting a word from one writing system to another, is a crucial component of many natural language processing (NLP) applications, including machine translation, information retrieval, and cross-lingual text mining. The goal of transliteration is to generate a target-language word that is phonetically equivalent to the source-language input, while also being a valid word in the target language. Recent approaches to transliteration have focused on discriminative character transduction, where a model is trained to predict the target-language characters given the source-language input. However, these approaches often rely solely on the source-language input and do not take into account the target-language context. In this paper, we present a discriminative substring decoder for transliteration, which extends recent approaches for discriminative character transduction by allowing for a list of known target-language words. This is an important resource for transliteration, as it provides additional context and constraints for the decoding process. Our approach is motivated by the observation that many transliteration tasks involve a limited vocabulary of common words, which can be used to inform the decoding process. By incorporating a list of known target-language words, our decoder can better capture the nuances of the target language and generate more accurate transliterations. Our decoder is based on a discriminative framework, where a model is trained to predict the target-language substrings given the source-language input and the list of known target-language words. The model is trained using a combination of features, including indicator features, which capture the presence or absence of specific characters or substrings, and hybrid generative features, which combine the strengths of generative and discriminative models. The hybrid generative features are based on a generative model of the target language, which provides a probability distribution over possible target-language words. This distribution is then used to inform the decoding process, by providing a prior probability over possible target-language substrings. We evaluate our decoder on a Japanese katakana-to-English transliteration task, where the goal is to convert Japanese words written in katakana script to their English equivalents. Our results show that our decoder achieves a 28.5% relative improvement in transliteration accuracy over the state-of-the-art decoder of Sherif and Kondrak (2007b). This improvement is due to the ability of our decoder to incorporate the list of known target-language words, which provides additional context and constraints for the decoding process.

Phrase reordering is a crucial component in statistical machine translation (SMT) systems, particularly for languages with significant word order differences, such as Chinese and English. Hierarchical phrase-based (HPB) translation has shown great promise in capturing both short and long distance phrase reorderings, thanks to its ability to represent a sentence as a hierarchical structure of phrases. However, conventional HPB systems often lack contextual information when performing phrase reorderings, which can lead to suboptimal translation results. The reordering decisions in HPB systems are typically made based on a set of pre-defined reordering rules, which are often simplistic and do not take into account the complex contextual relationships between phrases. To address this limitation, we propose a context-dependent phrase reordering approach that utilizes the maximum entropy (MaxEnt) model to help the HPB decoder select appropriate reordering patterns. The key idea behind our approach is to classify translation rules into several reordering patterns, and build a MaxEnt model for each pattern based on various contextual features. These features can capture important information about the surrounding phrases, such as their syntactic categories, semantic meanings, and positional relationships. By integrating the MaxEnt models into the HPB model, we can effectively guide the reordering process and improve the overall translation quality. The use of MaxEnt models for phrase reordering is motivated by their ability to handle complex, high-dimensional feature spaces and make probabilistic predictions based on the observed data. In our approach, we define a set of reordering patterns, such as monotone, swap, and insert, and build a separate MaxEnt model for each pattern. Each model is trained on a set of features that are extracted from the translation rules and the surrounding phrases. The features can include, for example, the part-of-speech tags of the phrases, their semantic roles, and the distances between them. During decoding, the MaxEnt models are used to predict the probabilities of each reordering pattern, given the current phrase and its context. The predicted probabilities are then used to guide the reordering process and select the most likely translation rules. Our approach has several advantages over conventional HPB systems. First, it can capture complex contextual relationships between phrases, which is essential for accurate phrase reordering. Second, it can handle a large number of features and make probabilistic predictions based on the observed data, which allows for more accurate and robust reordering decisions. Finally, it can be easily integrated into existing HPB systems, making it a practical and effective solution for improving translation quality.

Automatic keyphrase extraction is a fundamental task in natural language processing, which involves identifying the most important and representative phrases from a given document. The quality of keyphrase extraction systems is typically evaluated using metrics such as precision, recall, and F1-score, which measure the exact match between the extracted keyphrases and the reference keyphrases. However, these metrics have been criticized for being too strict, as they do not account for near-misses, where the extracted keyphrase is similar to the reference keyphrase but not identical. To address this limitation, researchers have proposed various n-gram-based evaluation metrics, which measure the similarity between the extracted keyphrases and the reference keyphrases at the n-gram level. These metrics have been widely used in other natural language processing tasks, such as machine translation and summarization, but their effectiveness in keyphrase extraction has not been thoroughly evaluated. This paper presents a feasibility study of n-gram-based evaluation metrics for automatic keyphrase extraction. We adapt various evaluation metrics, including BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE, which are commonly used in machine translation and summarization, to the keyphrase extraction task. We also investigate the R-precision evaluation metric, which is specifically designed for keyphrase evaluation. Our goal is to examine the effectiveness of these metrics in capturing the similarity between the extracted keyphrases and the reference keyphrases, and to identify the most suitable metric for keyphrase extraction. To evaluate the performance of these metrics, we use a standard keyphrase extraction dataset, which consists of a large collection of documents with manually annotated keyphrases. We apply each metric to the extracted keyphrases and calculate the correlation between the metric scores and the human annotations. Our results show that the R-precision metric achieves the highest correlation with human annotations, indicating that it is the most effective metric for evaluating keyphrase extraction systems.
